subject: EN
title: Reading Part 3: The village that switched off the night
source: Eigener Text im Aufgabenformat MSA Englisch (Reading Part 3: langer Artikel mit nummerierten Absätzen); Ort und Personen erfunden
body:
(1) When the street lights in Harlow Fell went out for the first time at midnight last March, Dorothy Pike stood at her bedroom window and counted. "I stopped at two hundred stars," the 71-year-old says. "Before that night, I could see perhaps twenty." Her village of 900 people in the north of England had just joined a growing number of places that are deliberately turning the night dark again.

(2) The idea did not come from star lovers. It came from the village council's accountant, who had noticed that lighting the empty streets between midnight and five in the morning was costing more than the council spent on its library. A trial was agreed: for one year, the lamps would be switched off during those five hours. The money saved would go to the library and the youth club.

(3) Not everybody was pleased. Sam Okoro, who runs the only pub, collected 140 signatures against the plan. "My staff walk home after closing time," he says. "Nobody asked them how they feel on a road they cannot see." Parents of teenagers were worried too, and one local newspaper predicted that burglars would be queuing up at the village sign.

(4) They were not. Police figures for the trial year show that the number of break-ins in Harlow Fell did not rise; it stayed exactly the same, at three. Officers were not surprised. Most burglaries, they point out, happen in the afternoon, when houses are empty, and a thief in a dark street needs a torch, which makes him easy to spot.

(5) The clearest winners of the experiment cannot sign petitions at all. Biologist Dr Hannah Whitlock has been counting moths in the village for six years. Under street lamps, she explains, the insects circle the light until they are exhausted, instead of feeding and visiting flowers. "In the dark year we caught nearly twice as many moths in our traps," she says. "And where there are moths, there are bats and birds that eat them. People think of bees when they think of flowers and fruit, but a lot of that work is done at night."

(6) Humans may benefit as well. Doctors have long warned that light at night confuses the body's inner clock and makes it harder to fall asleep. In a survey at the end of the trial, four out of ten villagers said they were sleeping better than before. Whitlock is careful with this number, though: "People who like the project may simply want it to be true. We asked for opinions. We did not measure anybody's sleep."

(7) What finally ended the argument was a compromise rather than a victory. The lamps on the road between the pub and the bus stop were fitted with sensors: they now stay off until somebody walks by, then light up for three minutes. The sensors used up about a third of the savings, but Okoro took down his petition. "I still think they should have talked to us first," he says. "But my staff get home safely, and I have to admit the sky is something special."

(8) Other councils are now writing to Harlow Fell to ask how it was done. Dorothy Pike's answer is short. "Don't start with the stars," she says. "Start with the people who are afraid of the dark. If you listen to them first, the stars will look after themselves."

title: Reading Part 3: Second-hand first
source: Eigener Text im Aufgabenformat MSA Englisch (Reading Part 3: langer Artikel mit nummerierten Absätzen); Ort und Personen erfunden
body:
(1) On a Saturday morning, the queue outside Threadbare in Millbrook reaches the corner of the street. Nobody in it is over twenty. When owner Priya Nair unlocks the door at ten, she has to let customers in ten at a time. "Fifteen years ago, people came in here quietly and hoped nobody from school would see them," she says. "Now they film themselves at the till."

(2) Used clothes have become fashionable, and the reasons are not hard to find. A second-hand jacket costs a fraction of a new one. It is often better made than the cheap fashion sold on the high street. And it is unlikely that anyone else in class will turn up wearing the same thing. For many young shoppers, however, the strongest argument is a different one: every item that is worn again is one that does not have to be produced, transported and, a few months later, thrown away.

(3) Sixteen-year-old Callum Reid is a typical customer. He has not bought anything new for a year, apart from socks and underwear. "Making one pair of jeans takes thousands of litres of water," he says. "My jeans already exist. That's the whole point." He finds most of his clothes in shops like Threadbare, and the rest on apps where people sell what they no longer wear.

(4) It is on these apps, though, that the trend shows its less attractive side. Some users have turned buying second-hand into a business. They get up early, buy the best pieces in charity shops for a few pounds and offer them online the same evening for five times the price. Nair sees them every week. "They are not doing anything illegal," she says. "But the people who really need a warm coat for five pounds now find an empty rail."

(5) There is a second problem. Because used clothes are cheap and feel like a good deed, it is easy to buy far too many of them. Dr Lena Hofmann, who studies shopping habits at the University of Millbrook, asked 300 teenagers to count the clothes in their wardrobes. Those who mostly bought second-hand owned more items, not fewer, than those who bought new. One in four pieces had been worn only once or never. "A T-shirt nobody wears has saved nothing," Hofmann says, "no matter where it was bought."

(6) Charity shops themselves are struggling with the boom in a way few customers notice. They receive more donations than ever, but much of it is cheap fashion that falls apart after a few washes and cannot be sold again. Sorting it and getting rid of it costs the shops money that was meant for their charity work.

(7) Hofmann does not want to spoil the fun. Buying used is still far better than buying new, she says. Her advice is simply to ask one question before paying: would I buy this at full price? If the answer is no, it should stay on the rail for someone else.

(8) Back at Threadbare, Callum has tried on a green wool coat, looked at himself in the mirror for a long time and put it back. "I've got a coat," he says, and shrugs. Priya Nair watches him leave without a bag. "That," she says, "is my favourite kind of customer. Don't tell my accountant."

subject: EN
title: Artikel: Nachbarschaftsprojekt „Suppe am Donnerstag“
body:
In der Lindenstraße in Leipzig riecht es jeden Donnerstag nach Gemüsesuppe. Ab 17 Uhr steht im **Hinterhof** der Nummer 12 ein großer Topf auf einem Gaskocher, und wer vorbeikommt, bekommt einen Teller – **kostenlos**. Die Idee hatte Hannelore Brandt, 68, früher Köchin in einer Schulkantine. „Ich wohne seit dreißig Jahren hier und kannte kaum einen Namen im Haus“, sagt sie. Das wollte sie ändern: Beim Essen sollen sich die **Nachbarn kennenlernen**.

Die Regel ist einfach: **Jeder bringt eine Zutat mit**, eine Zwiebel, drei Kartoffeln oder ein Bund Petersilie. Geschnippelt und gekocht wird **gemeinsam**. Das Brot vom Vortag **spendet** die Bäckerei an der Ecke, das Gas wird aus einer **Spendendose** bezahlt.

Bekannt wurde die Aktion durch **Handzettel**, die Kinder aus dem Haus in alle Briefkästen gesteckt haben. Inzwischen kommen jede Woche rund vierzig Leute. Besonders freut sich Brandt über **ältere Menschen, die allein leben**: „Manche haben seit Tagen mit niemandem gesprochen. Hier bleiben sie bis zum Abwasch.“
